q: For purposes of the 100-shareholder limit on S corporations, how are members of a family treated?
choices: All members of a family, including lineal descendants of a common ancestor and their spouses, are treated as one shareholder
Only a husband and wife may be treated as one shareholder
Each family member always counts as a separate shareholder
Family members count as one shareholder only if they live in the same household
exp: Members of a family (a common ancestor, lineal descendants within six generations, and their spouses and former spouses) are treated as one shareholder for the 100-shareholder limit. The rule is broader than the spousal rule alone.

q: Which of the following may be a shareholder of an S corporation?
choices: A partnership
The estate of a deceased individual
A nonresident alien individual
A C corporation
exp: Eligible shareholders are generally U.S. citizen or resident individuals, estates, and certain trusts and exempt organizations. Partnerships, corporations and nonresident aliens are ineligible, and any one of them owning shares disqualifies the corporation.

q: Cam Corp. has two classes of common stock that are identical in rights to distributions and liquidation proceeds, except that one class has voting rights and the other does not. May Cam elect S status?
choices: No, because it has more than one class of stock
No, unless the nonvoting shares are held by a single shareholder
Yes, because differences solely in voting rights do not create a second class of stock
Yes, but only if the nonvoting shares are less than 20% of the total
exp: An S corporation may have only one class of stock, but shares that differ only in voting rights are disregarded for that test. A true second class arises from differing rights to distributions or liquidation proceeds.

q: Dew Corp., a calendar-year C corporation, wants S status for the current year. It has had the same shareholders since January 1, and all of them consent. What is the latest date it may file Form 2553 for the election to be effective as of January 1 of the current year, absent relief for a late election?
choices: December 31 of the current year
The due date of the current year's return
April 15 of the current year
March 15 of the current year
exp: An election made by the 15th day of the third month of the tax year (March 15 for a calendar year) can be effective for that year; a later election takes effect the following year unless late-election relief applies. The return due date is not the election deadline.

q: Eve owns 40% of an S corporation. Her stock basis at the beginning of the year was $10,000. For the year her share of items was: ordinary business income $25,000, tax-exempt interest $2,000, nondeductible expenses $1,000, and cash distributions $15,000. What is her stock basis at year-end?
exp: Basis = $10,000 + $25,000 + $2,000 − $15,000 − $1,000 = $21,000. Tax-exempt income increases basis and nondeductible expenses decrease it; ignoring the tax-exempt interest gives $19,000 and ignoring the nondeductible expense gives $22,000.

q: Finn has an $8,000 basis in his S corporation stock and has lent the corporation $5,000. His share of the corporation's ordinary loss for the year is $20,000. How much of the loss may Finn deduct this year, assuming the at-risk and passive activity rules do not limit it?
exp: Losses are deductible first against stock basis ($8,000) and then against basis in loans the shareholder made directly to the corporation ($5,000), for $13,000; the remaining $7,000 is suspended and carried forward indefinitely. Stopping at stock basis gives $8,000.

q: Gil, the sole shareholder of an S corporation, personally guaranteed a $100,000 bank loan made to the corporation. The corporation has not defaulted. What effect does the guarantee have on Gil's basis for deducting losses?
choices: It increases his debt basis by $100,000
It increases his stock basis by $100,000
It has no effect until Gil actually makes payments on the guarantee
It increases his basis by his pro rata share of the loan
exp: A shareholder's guarantee of an entity loan does not create debt basis; only loans the shareholder makes directly to the S corporation (or payments made under the guarantee) count. Unlike a partnership, an S corporation's liabilities do not flow into shareholder basis.

q: In a prior year, Hana's basis in a loan to her S corporation was reduced by passed-through losses. This year the corporation has net income. How is the net increase applied?
choices: Entirely to stock basis
Pro rata between stock basis and debt basis
It is ignored until the loan is repaid
To restore debt basis first, then to increase stock basis
exp: A net increase in a later year first restores the reduced basis of the shareholder's loan (up to its face amount) and then increases stock basis. Restoring debt basis first matters because repayment of a loan with reduced basis produces gain.

q: An S corporation with a 365-day calendar year had ordinary business income of $365,000, earned evenly. Ann owned all 100 shares until she sold 50 shares to Ben, who is treated as owning them for the last 219 days of the year. No election to close the books was made. What is Ben's share of the ordinary income?
exp: Absent an election, items are allocated per share, per day: $365,000 ÷ 365 = $1,000 per day × 50% × 219 days = $109,500. Allocating half of the full year's income ($182,500) ignores that Ben owned shares for only part of the year.

q: Ivo is the sole shareholder of an S corporation that has never been a C corporation. After adjusting for the current year's income, his stock basis is $12,000. The corporation distributes $20,000 cash to him. How does Ivo treat the distribution?
choices: $20,000 dividend income
$12,000 tax-free and $8,000 capital gain
$12,000 dividend and $8,000 return of capital
$20,000 tax-free, with a negative basis of $8,000
exp: An S corporation with no accumulated E&P makes distributions that are tax-free to the extent of stock basis, and the excess, $20,000 − $12,000 = $8,000, is treated as gain from the sale of the stock. Basis cannot go below zero.

q: Jett Corp., an S corporation that was formerly a C corporation, has an accumulated adjustments account of $10,000 and accumulated E&P of $6,000. Its sole shareholder, whose stock basis is $30,000, receives a $20,000 cash distribution. How much of the distribution is a taxable dividend?
exp: Distributions come first from AAA ($10,000 tax-free, reducing basis), then from accumulated E&P ($6,000 dividend), and the last $4,000 is a tax-free return of basis. Concluding $0 because basis exceeds the distribution ignores the accumulated E&P layer.

q: Kilo Corp. converted from a C corporation to an S corporation three years ago. This year it sold an asset it owned on the conversion date and recognized a $50,000 net built-in gain, and the taxable income limitation does not reduce that amount. What built-in gains tax does Kilo owe?
exp: Built-in gains recognized within five years after conversion are taxed to the S corporation at the 21% corporate rate: 21% × $50,000 = $10,500. Answering $0 assumes S corporations never pay entity-level income tax.

q: An S corporation's election terminates because of excess passive investment income when the corporation:
choices: Has accumulated E&P from C corporation years at the end of each of three consecutive tax years and passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts in each of those years
Has passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts in any single year
Has passive investment income exceeding 50% of gross receipts for two consecutive years
Has any passive investment income while it has accumulated E&P
exp: Termination requires three consecutive years in which the corporation both has accumulated C corporation E&P at year-end and passive investment income exceeding 25% of gross receipts. A single year produces only the excess net passive income tax, not termination.

q: On July 1 of the current year, a shareholder of a calendar-year S corporation sold some of her shares to a partnership. What is the effect on the S election?
choices: The election terminates on January 1 of the following year
The election terminates on July 1, so the S short year ends June 30
The election terminates at the beginning of the current year
The election continues if the partnership's partners are all individuals
exp: When a corporation ceases to qualify, the election terminates on the date of the disqualifying event, and the day before is the last day of the S short year; a C short year follows. A partnership is an ineligible shareholder regardless of who its partners are.

q: A calendar-year S corporation has 1,000 shares outstanding, 400 of them nonvoting. Which group of shareholders may revoke the S election?
choices: Shareholders owning more than 50% of the voting shares only
Shareholders owning at least two-thirds of all shares
Shareholders owning more than 50% of all outstanding shares, voting and nonvoting
All shareholders unanimously
exp: A revocation requires consent of shareholders holding more than one-half of the outstanding shares, counting both voting and nonvoting stock. Unanimous consent is required to make an election, not to revoke one.

q: After an S election is terminated or revoked, how long must the corporation generally wait before making a new S election without IRS consent?
choices: One year
Three years
No waiting period applies
Until the fifth tax year beginning after the first year for which the termination was effective
exp: A corporation whose election terminated generally may not re-elect S status for five tax years unless the IRS consents. The one-year figure is a confusion with the post-termination transition period.

q: Which item of an S corporation is NOT separately stated on the shareholders' Schedules K-1?
choices: Depreciation on business equipment, other than §179 expense
Charitable contributions
Net long-term capital gain
Tax-exempt interest income
exp: Ordinary depreciation enters the computation of nonseparately stated ordinary business income. Charitable contributions, capital gains and tax-exempt income are separately stated because they may affect each shareholder's tax differently.

q: An S corporation pays health insurance premiums for Lin, an employee who owns 10% of its stock. How are the premiums treated?
choices: Excluded from Lin's income as a tax-free employee fringe benefit
Deductible by the corporation and included in Lin's wages, with Lin generally eligible for the self-employed health insurance deduction
Nondeductible by the corporation and treated as a distribution to Lin
Deductible by the corporation and exempt from income tax withholding and reporting
exp: A more-than-2% shareholder is treated like a partner for fringe benefit purposes, so premiums paid on his behalf are included in his W-2 wages (though not subject to FICA under these rules), and he may generally deduct them as self-employed health insurance. Tax-free fringe treatment applies only to employees owning 2% or less.

q: Moe is the sole shareholder and only employee of a profitable S corporation. He takes no salary and withdraws all profits as distributions. What is the most likely result if the IRS examines the corporation?
choices: No change, because S corporation distributions are never subject to payroll taxes
The distributions will be taxed as dividends at ordinary rates
The IRS may recharacterize a portion as reasonable wages subject to employment taxes
The S election will terminate
exp: A shareholder-employee who performs substantial services must be paid reasonable compensation, and the IRS can recharacterize distributions as wages subject to FICA and withholding. Avoiding employment tax does not terminate the election or create dividends.

q: Nan's S corporation stock basis at the beginning of the year was $10,000. For the year, her share of the ordinary loss was $12,000, and she received a $6,000 cash distribution. There were no income items. How much of the loss may she deduct this year?
exp: Basis is reduced by distributions before losses, so the $6,000 distribution is tax-free and leaves $4,000 of basis, which limits the loss deduction to $4,000; the remaining $8,000 is suspended. Applying the loss first would deduct $10,000 and make the distribution taxable.

q: Which statement about an S corporation's tax year is correct?
choices: It must use a calendar year unless it establishes a business purpose for a fiscal year or makes a §444 election
It may adopt any fiscal year without restriction
It must use the tax year of its largest shareholder, even if that is a fiscal year
It must use a fiscal year ending in September
exp: An S corporation must use a permitted year, which is the calendar year unless it establishes a business purpose (such as a natural business year) or elects a fiscal year under §444 with required payments. Free choice of fiscal year is a C corporation rule.

q: Which of the following taxes may be imposed on an S corporation itself?
choices: Accumulated earnings tax
Built-in gains tax
Personal holding company tax
Corporate alternative minimum tax on adjusted financial statement income
exp: An S corporation can owe entity-level tax on built-in gains, excess net passive income and LIFO recapture. The accumulated earnings and personal holding company taxes apply only to C corporations.

q: Ora formed an S corporation by transferring land with an adjusted basis of $40,000 and a fair market value of $70,000 for all of its stock in a transaction qualifying under §351. What is Ora's initial stock basis?
exp: S corporations are formed under the same §351 rules as C corporations, so Ora takes a substituted basis equal to the land's $40,000 basis. Fair market value would be used only if the exchange were taxable.

q: Pax had $15,000 of S corporation losses suspended for lack of basis when the corporation's S election terminated. How may Pax use the suspended losses?
choices: They are lost when the election terminates
They convert to a capital loss carryover
They may be deducted only against future C corporation dividends
They are deductible to the extent Pax increases stock basis by the end of the post-termination transition period
exp: Suspended losses are treated as incurred on the last day of the post-termination transition period (generally one year after the last S day, or later through the final return's extended due date), so Pax can deduct them by restoring stock basis, such as by contributing capital, before that period ends. Otherwise they are lost.

q: In applying limitations to an S corporation shareholder's share of a loss, what is the correct order?
choices: Basis limitation, then at-risk rules, then passive activity rules
Passive activity rules, then at-risk rules, then basis limitation
At-risk rules, then basis limitation, then passive activity rules
Basis limitation, then passive activity rules, then at-risk rules
exp: A loss must first clear the shareholder's stock and debt basis, then the at-risk rules of §465, and then the passive activity rules of §469 (with the excess business loss limit applied after that). Each limit applies only to the loss that survived the prior one.

q: Which statement about S corporations and subsidiaries is correct?
choices: An S corporation may not own stock of any other corporation
An S corporation may own 100% of a qualified subchapter S subsidiary, which is disregarded as a separate entity
An S corporation may own stock of a C corporation only if it owns less than 50%
A subsidiary owned by an S corporation automatically shares the parent's S election
exp: An S corporation may elect QSub treatment for a domestic corporation it wholly owns, and the QSub's items are treated as the parent's. It may also own any percentage of a C corporation; QSub status requires an election.

q: Which corporation is NOT eligible to elect S status?
choices: A domestic corporation with 75 shareholders, all U.S. citizens
A domestic corporation owned by a grantor trust
A foreign corporation
A domestic corporation that was a C corporation last year
exp: Only a domestic corporation that is not an ineligible corporation (such as certain financial institutions and insurance companies) may elect S status. A former C corporation and one owned by a grantor trust can qualify.

q: Quin's basis in his S corporation stock was $50,000 on January 1. He sold all of his shares on September 30 for $80,000. His share of the corporation's ordinary income through September 30 was $10,000, and he received no distributions. What is his gain on the sale?
exp: Basis is first increased by his $10,000 share of income through the sale date to $60,000, so gain = $80,000 − $60,000 = $20,000. Using the January 1 basis gives $30,000 and taxes the $10,000 of income twice.

q: Rae owns 50% of an S corporation and works full-time in its business. How is her $60,000 share of the corporation's ordinary business income treated for employment tax purposes?
choices: It is not subject to self-employment tax
It is subject to self-employment tax because she materially participates
It is subject to FICA withholding by the corporation
It is subject to self-employment tax only above her salary
exp: An S corporation shareholder's share of ordinary business income is not self-employment income; employment taxes apply only to wages actually paid. This differs from a general partner's distributive share, which is subject to SE tax.

q: Which statement about the accumulated adjustments account (AAA) of an S corporation is correct?
choices: It is maintained separately for each shareholder, like stock basis
It can become negative because of losses, but distributions cannot reduce it below zero
It is increased by tax-exempt income
It cannot become negative under any circumstances
exp: The AAA is a corporate-level account that is increased by income items other than tax-exempt income and decreased by losses and deductions, which can make it negative; distributions, however, cannot push it below zero. Stock basis, by contrast, is a shareholder-level figure that cannot go below zero.
